utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Good morning to the technical booth, the interpreters. Good morning to the staff of the registry, the counsel for the Prosecution, the counsel for the Defence. Good morning, General Krstic. We are resuming our hearing today, and I'm looking at the Defence to learn from them who will be the witness for today. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to my learned friends from the Prosecution. Your Honours, the Defence plans two witnesses for today. The first is our military expert, General Radinovic, who has already testified here in court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Usher, be kind enough to bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, General Radinovic. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We consider your testimony today to be a continuation of the testimony you made last time, so I am reminding you that you are testifying under oath, and having said that, I invite you to sit down. Thank you very much for coming. You will now be answering questions put to you by Mr. Visnjic. Mr. Visnjic, your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Visnjic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General Radinovic, can you tell Their Honours whether the Defence has asked you, after your testimony in the Defence case, in the break that we had until the beginning of the Prosecution case to review some allegedly intercepted conversations and to interpret their contents?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I ask the usher to show the witness Prosecution Exhibit 884, and also to prepare ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: If you can give the registrar one second to locate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, to save time, may I give the witness my copy of this exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Visnjic. I think that is a good idea. Thank you very much for your cooperation. I don't think that will be a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, we have before us Prosecution Exhibit 884 which the Prosecution contends is a conversation between Zivanovic, who is assumed to be General Zivanovic, and a certain Bogicevic. This conversation took place, according to what was stated, on the 15th of July, 1995, at 10.51 hours. As I do not have a copy with me now, would you be kind enough to read through this conversation for the transcript.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: The whole conversation?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, if possible, please.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: X and Y are speaking. According to this document, X has been identified as Bogicevic and Y as Zivanovic. "Good morning." Y replies, "Good morning." "Is Zivanovic there?" "He is and who is asking for him?" X: Bogicevic from Belgrade. Y: Just a moment. Z: Hello? X: Good morning...just a moment General, sir...someone for you. B: Hello. Z: Yes. B: Hi Zile. Z: Hi Bogi. B: And good luck. Or a pleasantry like that. Z: Thank you. B: Well I brought a truck...five tons of goods here in Ljubovija. And Ljubovija is on the right bank of the Drina on the Serbian side, a town in Serbia. Z: Yes. That's the same as if you were in Belgrade. B: Well, what should we do now? That's what Triso told me. Z: I beg your pardon? B: Triso told me so. Z: Triso doesn't know anything about borders, man. If that's what he said, inform him and give it to him. B: Are we going to bring anything? That is quite unintelligible. Z: Where? B: Up there, at your place. Z: I'm now in Belgrade. I liberated Srebrenica and now I have got a new duty. B: Yes, yes... Good. Z: How are you doing? B: Excellent. I'll come up there. Z: I've nowhere else to go. B: I'll come up there now to bring you some watermelons... so you can refresh yourself. Z: Okay. Okay. B: Yes. Z: How are my Serbian people? B: Good. And then a word that can't be read. Z: Everything is okay... Say hello to the Serbs. B: I will... Go on, talk to you later. Z: Take care. B: Goodbye. And that is the end of the conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, for a better understanding, General Radinovic, on page 3, line 17 and 18, made a comment as to where the town of Ljubovija is, and I want to make this clear for the transcript. So page 3, lines 17 and 18, were General Radinovic's comments.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, what is relevant in this conversation in relation to all the events around Srebrenica and in relation to your previous testimony?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: In the context of all the events that we are testifying about here, and in the context of my previous testimony, there's only one sentence that is relevant, and that is the 29th sentence, if I counted the lines correctly, in which General Zivanovic says, and allow me to quote: "I liberated Srebrenica and now I have got a new duty," or, "I've been given a new duty." Why do I think that this is important for the events we are discussing? Because in the first part of this sentence, General Zivanovic claims that he liberated Srebrenica, and in my judgement, thereby he resolves all dilemmas as to who was in command of the forces engaged in Krivaja 95, that is, in the operation for Srebrenica. He says he liberated Srebrenica, and thereby he himself clearly states that he was in command. And in the second part of the sentence, General Zivanovic declares that, "Now I have been given a new assignment," "now." In the Serbian language, the word "now" means just now, the time that immediately precedes this conversation. Because there are other terms that have similar meanings, which are synonymous, like "today" or "recently" or "a short while ago." But when you say "now," that really means the time in the immediate vicinity of this -- of the time of this conversation, and that is this conversation between Bogicevic and Zivanovic, the 15th of July, at 10.51 hours. So it means that he had only just been assigned a new duty. For me, who has been a witness in these proceedings, this statement is vital because it removes all dilemmas as to who was, at least up to the 15th of July, at 10.51, the commander of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General Radinovic, where was General Zivanovic when he was conducting this conversation, on the assumption that the conversation is authentic, as well as its content?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: From what is said in the conversation, one could infer that he was in Belgrade, but that is not what the whole context tells us. This is clearly not in Belgrade. If he was in Belgrade, he would not be using this line, but another line, and Bogicevic, as a man who is doing something for the needs of the Drina Corps, would not go all the way from Belgrade to Bosnia-Herzegovina without informing himself as to the whereabouts of General Zivanovic. Taking into consideration all the events that preceded this time when this conversation is assumed to have taken place, he is without doubt at the command post in Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, General. Could I ask the usher to prepare for the witness Defence Exhibits D167, D168 and Defence Exhibit D169, as well as OTP Exhibit 446. Your Honours, this is a Defence exhibit, 167. It is a telephone conversation which was identified during the testimony by Ms. Stefanie Frease, Prosecution witness, and during the testimony a date was set, as was the time when this intercepted conversation was allegedly conducted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, I should take the liberty of reading out this conversation. It is a conversation between Uran, a person "X," and Colonel Cerovic. U: Uran (Obrad). X: Uran. All right... You are connected. U: Hello. C: Uran. U: How are you, boss? C: Well, okay. And how are you, Rade? U: Not bad. Not bad. Listen, please. C: Hello. U: Listen. C: Wait till I get to another phone. I can't hear a word you are saying. U: Go ahead. C: I am listening. U: Krstic in person ordered it and so did 01. C: Yes. U: This convoy bound for Kladanj ... C: Yes? U: (Interference). C: All right. U: (Interference) That no one has the right to do anything (interference). C: All right. U: And also literally that we are to behave in a civilised fashion and that everyone is to behave like that so that nothing of the kind of problem we had before happens. C: All right. U: Please call those public security stations, call the commanders of the units who are there, call everybody who is responsible for ensuring that everything runs smoothly and (unintelligible). C: All right. U: That's it, boss. C: When will they set out, Obrad? U: I don't know. I can't tell you when they're leaving, but take measures immediately. C: Okay. U: Take measures immediately. Call and be sure to know exactly to which persons you transmitted it, the most responsible ones, and following up implementation through the officer on duty. C: All right. U: That's it, boss. C: Cheers. U: Sure. Good luck. General, according to the contention of the Prosecution, this conversation was conducted on the 25th of July, 1995. Within the context of which events could we place this conversation?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I understand it, the time when this conversation was conducted should be set within the context of the events in Zepa, because on the 25th the evacuation of civilians from Zepa started.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General Radinovic, allow me to read out a second conversation now, conducted, according to the Prosecution's submission, on the same day, that is, the 25th of July, at 1319 hours. The participants in this conversation are Colonel Cerovic and Djuric. C: Milovan? It is Defence Exhibit D168. C: Milovan? D: Djuric speaking. C: Who? D: Djuric. C: Ilija? D: Yes. C: So you are in your area of responsibility. D: Yes. C: It must all be done without any stopping, without searches, even at the cost of shooting those who would try to threaten that convoy. D: All right. C: Now, be so kind as to call Markovic at the SUP and tell him that this is an order of the state president, that together with us, in their area of responsibility, up there along their border with the people from Sokolac, they too are to deliver this safely to the guys in Sokolac. D: All right. C: Do you understand? D: (Inaudible). C: Well, call me to say whether Markovic received the message. Call the officer on duty here. D: All right. I think that he is in the field, he has other tasks, but I will convey it there and I will call. C: Well, all right. D: All right. C: Cheerio. General, taking into consideration that these two conversations took place within a 20-minute time span on the same day, may I be free to conclude that they refer to the same subject, that is, the transport of the civilian population from Zepa?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is how I understand it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the previous conversation, the sentence that says, "Krstic personally has ordered it and so has O1," General, who could Krstic be in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: If we look at the header, at the beginning of the conversation who the participants are, Uran and Zeric, Uran is the code-name for the forward command post of the Drina Corps. And in brackets it says "Obrad," so I assume it was Obrad Vicic, Assistant Chief of Staff in the Drina Corps who, by nature of things, should have been at the time at the forward command post because this was taking place at the time of the Zepa operation. So in view of that fact, there is no question that it could be anyone else but General Krstic who was in command of the operative group for Zepa at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who is 01, General?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: In marking persons by numbers in the chain of command in our army, in my army, and a similar practice was applied by the VRS, 01 is the code given to the Supreme Commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was the Supreme Commander?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: The Supreme Commander of the army of Republika Srpska was Radovan Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that fit into this second sentence from Exhibit 168 when Cerovic says to a certain Djuric, "Convey to him that this is an order of the president of the state"?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that fully fits into the contents of the conversation conducted 20 minutes earlier. Cerovic is conveying the message given to him by Uran, and that is General Krstic. He is conveying to the person who is to execute the order, that is Djuric, and he is giving greater emphasis to that order by saying that this is an order given by the president of the state.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, in your testimony, a member of the investigating team of the Prosecution -- I'm sorry, in her testimony, Ms. Stefanie Frease stated that orders of this kind, such as were allegedly given by Krstic in this conversation, were the consequence of the focussed attention of world public opinion on the events in Zepa, or rather, the events in the enclaves, and all this because the events in Srebrenica had already become known to the International Community. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: I do not agree that that prompted this order from Krstic, nor do I consider it to be the main reason for this contact in this way. Of course, in the media there were various reports about these things. It had still not been established with certainty that this had happened, and it is very difficult to make any conclusions as to whether such information had reached the people who had participated in the Zepa operation and particularly those in charge of that operation, whether such news had reached them at all, particularly in view of the circumstances under which they were conducting the operation, they had very little contact with public opinion in general. I couldn't allege that they hadn't heard anything, but certainly not to such an extent that they would explain orders of this kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I ask the usher to give the witness OTP 446, please. Your Honours, this is a conversation between a person named as Krstic and a certain Sobot conducted, according to the submission of the Prosecution, on the 12th of July, 1995, at 1305 hours. Mr. President, I shall read this conversation out, too, in view of a minor discrepancy in the translation, so I shall be free to ask the General to comment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So Krstic, Sobot: K: How many buses have started out from down there? S: 20. K: Fine, 20. S: And the others are on the way? K: On the road, good. S: ... K: Put me back to the switchboard. Miss, put me through to the Vlasenica Brigade. C: Yes. K: This is Krstic. C: Can I help you, General? K: Give me Kosrovic. C: He's not here, he went somewhere. K: Give me Savo, put me through to Savo. S: How are you General? This is Savo. K: Srpski, fuck it, how else. S: Congratulations, fuck ... K: Get in touch with these guys from the MUP, that means you, your brigade and them. S: I gave everything there is. K: Wait, slow down, man, secure the road, from the crossroad below, from where you are, 12 kilometres towards Drava and up to the tunnel. S: To the tunnel? K: Of course. S: Okay. K: That's where they'll be disembarking. S: Okay. K: Take care nothing must happen to any of them. S: Okay. K: Is that clear? S: Yes, sir. K: Until further notice, secure that part of the road. S: Okay. K: That's it chief, bye. S: Bye. General, the sentence, "Take care that --" in the translation it says, "Nothing must happen to them," Defence counsel says, "Not a hair must be touched on their heads," if we translate it literally, "No one's hair on his head may be touched." What kind of an order is that, General?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, this is a saying, a metaphor. When you say, "Not a hair must be hurt on his head," it's the highest degree -- the greatest emphasis on the protection of the safety of the person to whom this applies, because as we know, we lose hairs from our heads all the time. So when you say this, when you use this expression, it is a strict requirement and it means that absolutely the slightest thing may not happen to that person. So this applies to the people who will appear from Srebrenica on the road, from Srebrenica to Kladanj at the spot where their disembarkation is planned and their transfer to the territory under the control of the Muslim authorities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, if I say, "Nothing must happen to him," and then I say, "Not a hair may be harmed on their heads," by saying that, am I making this statement much stricter, giving it much greater emphasis? Am I right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, on the 12th of July, 1995, the International Community was certainly not familiar with the events in Srebrenica as they occurred later?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: No, they were not aware of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be given Defence Exhibit 169 now, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the exhibit be placed on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, sir, these are portions of the conversation that we've already discussed, the 12th of July conversation which quotes the alleged statement made by General Krstic, and the conversations on the 25th of July in which, once again, orders are being quoted that General Krstic allegedly issued.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I should just like to draw the attention of the Trial Chamber to the sentence uttered on the 12th of July, that is to say, the translation is basically correct, but translated literally this sentence reads, "Not a hair of their heads must be harmed." That is the translation of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now we have the statement of General Krstic allegedly on the 12th of July and on the 25th of July, his alleged sentences uttered on that date. What does that indicate to you?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: These conversations, when you link them up, and this document, too, this indicates to me, this leads me to think that there was continuity of a persistent expression of General Krstic's resolute stand and proper conduct towards the civilian population. In the same way that in combat documents he always strove to ensure that the civilian population was not the target of attack, so also in these particular documents, if these conversations are authentic, of course, General Krstic once again is striving for and issuing orders to his subordinates that civilian population cannot be the target of any kind of retaliation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, sir, in Exhibit 167 there is a sentence which Uran says to Cerovic, and it says, it reads, "We must behave in a civilised manner and everybody must behave in that way so that nothing of the kind of problem we had before happens." What does that mean, General, sir?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: It means that Colonel Cerovic, and Colonel Cerovic is the assistant for morale, legal issues, religious issues of the corps, that is to say, Colonel Cerovic conveys -- is conveying an order which he himself received. He is fully conscious of the fact that during the time that the population left Srebrenica, they behaved in an uncivilised fashion, and he draws attention to the fact that this should not happen again. And luckily, it did not happen again to the civilians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, General, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the Defence has no further questions. Just one more, actually, just one small question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, sir, when we gave you these conversations for comment, to hear your comments, you explained to us that you didn't like to comment on intercepted conversations of this kind. Would you just repeat some of the reasons you gave for this to us; why do you not like to comment?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: In my examination-in-chief when I testified before this august Tribunal, I put forward the reasons. I said why, in the preparation for my expert finding, I did not use the intercepts and why I could not consider them to be evidence and exhibits. And I wasn't happy that you made me comment on the exhibits which I did not qualify as being exhibits myself. I was not able to accept them as such, and thereby you made me deviate from my stand of principle. But thank you for asking me that question now to be able to explain myself and to justify myself for doing so before this Tribunal and all the distinguished people here. For me, an intercepted conversation of any kind is only an intimation of, an announcement of a possible -- of possible evidence, and this must only be a source for quest; that is to say, you will have to enter into a quest for evidence which can bear out the hypothesis which relates to the events that are being scrutinised. For me to be able to consider an intercepted conversation instead of just an illusion and intimation or a clue or hint, for me to be able to accept that as a fact, as a confirmation of a fact, and thereby to consider these intercepted conversations as evidence and as an exhibit, I would have to conduct very many complicated actions and costly activities, costly steps as foreplay, so to speak, which would raise the intercepted conversations to the level of evidence and thereby, by the same token, the level of an actual exhibit. We would have to conduct -- have a register of all the intercepted conversations. All the intercepted conversations would have had to be classified in what we call statistic series, according to precisely defined and criteria accepted by the experts themselves. After that, experts for samples of this kind would compile a stratified sample in order to determine the authenticity of the conversations intercepted, and this procedure, as I say, is a highly complex one. For all these conversations and the way they were taking them down, you must have a phonetic record. We must be able to determine the correspondence between what exists on the tape and what is written out as a text, as a transcript. If we determine absolute authenticity of all the conversations intercepted contained in the sample, then we can enter a new phase, a new stage of interpretation on the part of experts of the conversations, and then this will bring them closer to the level of evidence and exhibit. But if we ascertain that if in a sample only one -- even one conversation is not authentic, then we must have to resort to the method of complete induction, which means to encompass all the intercepted conversations and to study each and every one to see if they are authentic or not. So as you can see, the procedure is highly complex, enormous in scope and scale. It is a long-winded form of research requiring multidisciplinary procedure. You would have to have experts of different profiles called in, strategists, military experts, people -- experts in informatics, linguists, stylists, and so on and so forth, people of -- experts of different profiles, profiles that I myself might not be aware of. And this would be a very lengthy process. So as I myself was not capable of undertaking an investigation of that kind - I am not professionally trained for things of that kind, neither did I have enough time. It would be very costly and time-consuming - that is why I considered all the intercepts that I had at my disposal to be -- I read them through, but I was not able to class them as evidence and thereby exhibits. And it is a great pity that this was not done in such a way. It could have been done, and it would be much easier for us to be able to ascertain the truth had the whole process been gone through, and that is why I say I did not like to comment on these exhibits, because you're asking me to make an assertion. I have to draw conclusions on the basis of these conversations. But I set my limits, and I said that at the beginning of my testimony, that I was very unwilling to make any observations or conclusions of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, General, sir. Your Honours, the Defence has no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Visnjic. General, how is your voice today? Is it better?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, thank you for inquiring about my voice. In Serbian we have a metaphor which says, "I've lost my good voice," meaning my reputation or my throat. Now, I have said that I've lost my good voice and it's up to you to interpret it. But anyway, thank you for asking. Unfortunately, I can't say that my throat is in very good condition. I am at the end of my tether, I might say, on the downhill in my life, but we're doing what we can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Would you like to take a break, having said that, before we continue? Shall we take a break before we come to your cross-examination, General Radinovic? Would you like a break at this point?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: I can answer. I can go on answering. If I need a break for my throat, perhaps I'll ask for one. My Defence counsel asked to read the conversations. I would prefer not to have to read conversations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, General. Then we shall continue. Mr. Cayley, it is your witness now.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Good morning. Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours. General, I have to say that I didn't think that we would ever be reunited in this lifetime, but fate has its way and here we are again, but I think this will be a fairly short cross-examination. If the witness could be given Prosecutor's Exhibit 884, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I hope you're happy to see me again. I hope it's not the other way around. I'm happy to see you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Of course, General. Of course I'm happy to see you. Cross-examined by Mr. Cayley:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this, General, is the intercept of the 15th of July. Your Honours, this is the intercept between Bogicevic and Zivanovic of the 15th of July. And I wanted you to concentrate on one particular sentence, first of all, and that is the sentence which you alluded to last -- in your examination-in-chief, where Zivanovic states: "I liberated Srebrenica and now I've got a new duty." Now, General, you would agree with me that when Zivanovic was stating that he had liberated Srebrenica, this was pure bravado on his part, was it not?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't agree with you there. It wasn't just bravado. And all my research testifies to the fact that General Zivanovic was right. He was actually saying that. And the whole concept -- when we speak of Srebrenica, we also use a metaphoric expression and say "the liberation of Srebrenica," but here I think he is expressing his position and saying that he was commanding the Srebrenica operation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, this Court has heard evidence from an officer who was present at the forward headquarters at Pribicevac, from where the Srebrenica operation was being conducted, and that is Witness DB. And let me read to you his testimony, and this is on page 7221, and the question from my learned friend, Mr. Harmon: " Q. Did it appear to you that General Zivanovic had an important role in commanding the operation against Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: According to my recollection, he didn't interfere significantly with the command of the operation, but that the operation Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. initially, up to the 9th, was under the command of General Krstic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So up to the 9th, General Zivanovic did not play an important role in directing and commanding the attack?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: No." Now, General, you would agree with me that an officer, senior VR officer, who was present at the forward headquarters would know far better than you who was commanding the operation to take Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, no, he doesn't know better than me. I know better than him. It was a protected witness, so I'm not sure who the witness was. And for these purposes it's not essential either, although it would be important to see what rank he held during the Srebrenica operation. But I can conclude that General Zivanovic was commanding the forces at Zepa, and I do so on the basis of relevant facts. The first fact is that he signed the combat order for active operations of Krivaja 95, and you can take a look at the documents and exhibits and you will find that that is so. Secondly, he himself in this conversation says that he liberated Srebrenica. Thirdly, on the videotape which was -- has become an exhibit here, Prosecution exhibit, General Zivanovic can be seen, together with General Mladic, the Main Staff commander; General Krstic as the Chief of Staff of the Drina Corps; and another group of officers from the Drina Corps. He was seen on the 11th of July, upon entrance into Srebrenica. So there is no reason for us to say that somebody else was in command and that not the de facto Corps Commander, if there are no indices of that kind, official or unofficial documents to that effect. The impression that might be gained by that particular officer who testified before this Tribunal that up to the 9th General Zivanovic was not the commander of the forces for Srebrenica, was probably based on the fact that it is the right of the Corps Commander, according to his own assessment of the situation, to be at different parts of the front and to control different parts of the front. This is left to his discretion. And the command post or points for command are organised and placed so that you are able to command the whole area of responsibility. And the Drina Corps commander had his forward command post, and the forward command post is an ad hoc command post for a certain operation. Forward command posts are not placed in this forward position for other bodies but for himself. So it is his forward command post.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, stop, stop, stop. You're not answering the question, and I'm not going to spend the next two hours with you not answering the question. Would you agree with me that when General Zivanovic ceased to be the commander of the Drina Corps is an absolutely critical aspect of this case? Do you agree with that proposition?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think I can share your opinion and say -- put it that way. General Zivanovic received a decree on the 15th of July --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, that's not the question I asked you. The question I asked you is this: Do you agree with me that in this case, the date upon which General Zivanovic ceased to be the commander of the Drina Corps is fundamental, it is a fundamental fact in this case? Do you agree with that proposition?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think the General is now being asked to make legal interpretations. Perhaps I'm wrong, but that is what it seems to me to be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Radinovic is an expert witness, Mr. Visnjic, so he is able to give an opinion, and Mr. Cayley is asking him a question. We will have the General's answer to that question. Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, is it or is it not an important part of this case the date upon which General Zivanovic ceased to be the commander of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: You mean this piece of paper or the whole case?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me put it in a more straightforward fashion. I'm obviously not being clear about this. Do you agree with me, the document aside, generally speaking, do you agree with me that the date upon which General Zivanovic ceased to be the commander of the Drina Corps is an important fact in this entire case? Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, did you meet with General Zivanovic in February or March of last year?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember the exact date, but yes, I did meet with him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me read to you a question put to you by Her Honour Judge Wald, and your answer: "JUDGE WALD: In your discussion with General Zivanovic, did you ever ask him directly when he relinquished his command, on what date he stopped being commander, leaving the document and the handover ceremony aside?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: You didn't -- in your conversation with him, you didn't ask him, even though it was apparent in February or March, from the early pre-trial documents of the Prosecution, that this was a critical point for them? You didn't ask him when he stopped being commander?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: I had no doubt in my mind that he was Drina Corps commander during the Srebrenica operation, and I focused my attention on that operation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: All right. Just to tie this down: You and he never discussed specifically when he said he stopped being commander. That's what you just said; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: We did not discuss it." And that is on page 8385 of the LiveNote transcript. General, don't you agree with me that it is somewhat ridiculous that you come here giving your opinions and interpretation on intercepts when you had the opportunity to ask Zivanovic himself when he ceased to be the commander of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: Please don't use words of that kind. I have come here upon the request of the Defence to comment on the intercepts. As I say, I did so very unwillingly, for the reasons I put forward.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, answer my question. Would any normal expert have asked General Zivanovic when he ceased to be the commander of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: I had the document on the appointment of General Krstic and General Zivanovic, with the 15th of July date, and I considered that that is incontestable and that I would very easily be able to get to the records and minutes of the handing over of duty and that this would be very easy to ascertain when one relinquished his command to the other. And the fact that I didn't ask at that particular point in time, it could have been a methodological mistake, but at that moment I didn't think that it was essential, important. I thought that we would see each other again and be able to ascertain that question, and I thought the Prosecution had the document anyway and that it would be very easy to ascertain. Now, it turned out that the Prosecution did not have this document, and unfortunately I did not get the document either, whereas I thought that all the participants in this case had the document, that the archives of the Drina Corps had it, that General Krstic and Zivanovic had this document, and in the cadres' department. But unfortunately that document doesn't seem to be anywhere. I haven't got it. So it was up to us to speculate from the 15th onwards. But there is the decree by the supreme commander saying that it could not have been before the 15th of July. So for me that was an incontestable fact, something that I didn't think I needed to go into and check out when I saw General Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you spend with General Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: Is that important for these proceedings? If it is, I can tell you that it was --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, I will decide what questions are important. Please just answer questions directly that I put to you. It's for the President to intervene if he feels that my questions are irrelevant, not for you. How many hours did you spend with General Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't count the hours, of course, but we spent a certain amount of time before lunch and some time after lunch, which means, let's say, one working day, but I can't tell you the exact number of hours. And during that conversation of ours, I allowed General Zivanovic, gave him the opportunity, to tell me about the operative situation with respect to Srebrenica, which was the most important thing for me, and that is why perhaps I omitted to go into some questions that are vital to this case. But there you have it. It was an omission, and I suppose many omissions are committed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you spent an entire day with General Zivanovic, and during that day you never asked him the date upon which he relinquished command of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not ask him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's a fact, isn't it, General, that he told you on that day that he relinquished command of the Drina Corps on the 13th [Realtime transcript read in error "15th"] of July? He told you, didn't he, on that day, that that's the day he relinquished command?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: No. No. He didn't. Not even on that day. No, he didn't tell me about the 15th [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's move on. I'm not going to re-cross-examine you on all of the documents on this issue, because we'll be here for a week.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If Prosecutor's Exhibit 30 could be made available. Mr. President, I don't know whether you wish to take a break at this point, or I can continue. It's as you wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we can actually have a break at this point. We will have a 20-minute break now, not a half-hour break, but a 20-minute break only.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, while the witness is being brought in, there needs to be a correction to the transcript. At line 21, my question is stated, "It's a fact, isn't it, General, that he told you on that day that he relinquished command of the Drina Corps on the 15th of July." My question continues, and the witness answers no. In fact, I asked the witness, this is exactly what I said, "It's a fact, isn't it, General, that he told you on that day that he relinquished command of the Drina Corps on the 13th of July." The rest of it is correct, it's just the date was incorrect, so I just correct that so the transcript is accurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I noted it down "13."

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Riad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I, too, heard the 13th in the interpretation. What did the Defence hear, so that we can hear the other party as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, if the answer was no, then it's all the same to us. Yes, yes. The date was the 13th, actually, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. The record will be corrected. We have a lot of witnesses in the courtroom. You may continue, Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, before you came here to give evidence today, knowing that you would be speaking about the day on which Zivanovic relinquished command, did you get in contact with Zivanovic to discuss the matter with him before you testified?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: You mean for the purposes of this testimony?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So knowing full well it was important in November of last year, and knowing full well that it was important, absolutely critical in coming back here to give rejoinder evidence, you never made any attempt to contact General Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did, but General Zivanovic is inaccessible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where is General Zivanovic, General?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's move on. Now, General, you said in your examination-in-chief today that news of what had happened in the Srebrenica enclave and the executions that had happened immediately after the taking of the territory was not well known enough by the 25th of July for those VRS individuals in Zepa to be aware of those facts. Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: That's not exactly what I said. I said that there were news about it in the media; however, the question was whether the news could reach the members of the VRS in Zepa, in particular, those who were conducting the operation in view of the circumstances of the operation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, I'm going to just refer briefly to Prosecutor's Exhibit 30. It's the report of the Secretary-General on the fall of Srebrenica. It's in English, but I know from your evidence last year that you have read this particular report, and let's see what His Excellency Kofi Annan says about the status of news about Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And I'm going to quote, Mr. Usher, from paragraph 388. And I will read sections of it, Your Honours. I'm not going to read all of it, but I would direct you to paragraph 388 onwards of that report on page 84. Paragraph 388 reads as follows: "As of 17 July," and it's referring to 17 July 1995, "the BSA continued to refuse --" Yes, that's fine, Mr. Usher "-- continued to refuse to honour the agreements related to Srebrenica which Mladic had entered into in Belgrade two days earlier. The special representative of the Secretary-General reported to New York that day that the status and location of unaccounted-for persons and possible detainees, especially draft-age males, remains a large gap in our database. Unconfirmed reports provide accounts of detention centres, execution-style murder, rapes of young women, and other atrocities." We'll move to paragraph 389: "The same day, one of the DutchBat soldiers, during his brief stay in Zagreb, upon return from Serb-held territory, was quoted as telling a member of the press that hunting session is in full swing. It is not only men supposedly belonging to the Bosnian government who are targeted. Women, including pregnant ones ..." and he goes on. I won't quote all of what is said. On the sentence on the next page, this is continuing with 389 and it's referring to the story of the DutchBat witness: "The story was picked up by a number of wire services and reproduced. At approximately the same time, survivors of executions had also begun to recount their testimonies to the international and local press." And then in paragraph 390, and this is the final part that I'll read: "This prompted the secretariat to write to the special representative the following day, 18 July 1995: 'You will no doubt have read and heard the extensive reports of atrocities committed by the Bosnian Serbs during their recent takeover of Srebrenica.'" And I won't read on. General, by the 18th of July, you heard Kofi Annan, you heard about allegations of atrocities, the special representative of the Secretary-General knew, and the airwaves were positively buzzing with reports of what had happened in Srebrenica. Now, it's a fact, isn't it, General, that by the 25th of July, the VRS in Zepa knew exactly what had happened in Srebrenica? They've heard all of these reports, haven't they?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure that all of them heard those reports; and then, second, I am sure that many of them didn't know what had happened there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, let's look at Prosecutor's Exhibit 883, which is a new Prosecution exhibit. General, this is directive, operational directive number 4 from the Main Staff of the army of RS. It's dated the 19th of November of 1992. I am only interested in a direction given to the Drina Corps. You will find that in your version on -- I think it's page 6. The number is up in the top right-hand corner. The evidence number is 00876282.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, it's on page 5 of the English version. I think my learned friend, Mr. Visnjic, has a comment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Visnjic. Let us hear your comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this is a document the Defence has objected to, that the document be used as evidence during the testimony of Mr. Rick Butler. After we made this objection to the use of this document, the Prosecutor withdrew the document and no longer wanted Mr. Butler to speak about it. This is an extensive document, both in terms of its content and its length. And secondly, it does not refer to the subject we are currently discussing and the subject which General Radinovic testified about. It doesn't concern the facts alleged in the indictment either. And my learned colleague is now trying to tender this into evidence in this way. This document was issued in 1992, and as I have already indicated, it's a very large, extensive document. It's also a very complex document, in view of its contents. Therefore, Mr. President, I don't know if my learned colleague wishes to question the witness about this document. He can do so, but without explicit reference to this document, to which we object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think there's two issues that my learned friend has identified: First of all relevance, how is it relevant to General Radinovic's testimony; and second, admissibility. I'm going to have to consult with my colleagues on the point of admissibility. I'll clarify that with Mr. McCloskey. But as to relevance, the only section of this document to which I wish to refer is that which concerns orders given to the Drina Corps in respect of operations against Zepa. Now, General Radinovic himself has spoken specifically about events in Zepa, and I believe that this particular document is relevant to that point. As to admissibility, if you would give me a moment and I will just speak with Mr. McCloskey. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. My apologies. My understanding is that the Defence have had this document since February of 2001, and it was disclosed to them in accordance with agreements that were made between the Defence and the Prosecution to have continuing disclosure of relevant material, material relevant to this case. It was excluded from Mr. Butler's -- or they made an objection to exclude it from Mr. Butler's testimony, because when Mr. McCloskey had given a description of Mr. Butler's evidence, the proposed evidence, this particular matter, this document, the subject matter was inadvertently missed out from that description. So the Defence essentially said: We were not on notice that he was going to testify about this matter, so we therefore object to this particular document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Visnjic, do you wish to reply?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do, Mr. President. The first and foremost reason for our objection to this document is the fact that it refers to the events which took place in 1992, the events which have never been the subject of the discussions before this Chamber in this case. Second, we're dealing here with the events which require a broader approach and detailed analysis. In our previous objection, we explained to the Court why we consider ourselves to be unprepared for the use of this document. If the Prosecution wishes to use the documents from this period of time, then the Defence must require additional time to prepare, regardless of the fact to what extent the document needs to be used. So we have to require additional time for preparation. Third, I still do not see the link, even in the paragraph that Mr. Cayley wishes to use, I don't see the link with the testimony of General Radinovic, except if we're not talking about Zepa as a link, which is used in both cases. So I think that by using the documentation from some other period of time, we will go far beyond the scope of this testimony, and we will have to require additional time to prepare ourselves for the document. The document has been disclosed to us, that is true, but some other binders containing a large amount of documents have also been disclosed. And in view of the subject of the testimony of General Radinovic, and also in view of the subject which was raised by the Prosecution, we are -- this actually refers to the testimony of Ms. Frease, and Ms. Frease didn't mention at any point in time the year 1992 or the Zepa operation or the operation in which the Drina Corps was involved. We are dealing with the year 1995, and the role of the Drina Corps in those events. If the Prosecutor wishes to extend the subject matter, we do not have anything against it, it's just that we have to be given additional time to prepare ourselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me consult with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Cayley, we will hear your question, and then we will make a ruling whether or not we will hear the response.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, do you have the page that I was speaking about in front of you, which is ...

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but it's a very poor copy. I can hardly see what it says.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me read to you paragraph D.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And this, Mr. Usher, is on page 5 at the bottom so the public can see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll read it, and this is an order from General Mladic to the Drina Corps: "From its present positions, its main forces shall persistently defend --"

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I haven't heard that portion of the text. I cannot see it on page 6 here.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, you have it in front of you now. I'll read it. "The Drina Corps: From its present positions, its main forces shall persistently defend Visegrad, Zvornik, and the corridor, while the rest of its forces in the wider Podrinje region shall exhaust the enemy, inflict the heaviest possible losses on him and force him to leave the Birac, Zepa, and Gorazde areas together with the Muslim population. First offer the able-bodied and armed men to surrender, and if they refuse, destroy them. After that, unblock and repair the Konjevic Polje-Zvornik road, make it fit for traffic, and stand by for intensive combat against infiltrated sabotage, terrorist, surprise, and ambush attacks and paramilitary groups." And I won't read the remainder. Now, General, this is an order from General Mladic from 1992, and you would agree with me that his intention then was that the civilian population should be forced to leave the Zepa area, was it not, from this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we hear the response, let me consult with my colleagues for the ruling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber notes that even the Defence has asked questions regarding this period of time. The Chamber has also asked questions concerning the same time framework in order to understand the situation in Srebrenica. The Chamber and the parties considered some previous events in previous periods of time as well. So there was a time which preceded the relevant times, and it is necessary for us to hear the response in order to understand the overall question. The Chamber has therefore decided to let General Radinovic answer the question.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: Would you please repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course, General. Based on this document where General Mladic states, essentially, "Force him," the enemy, "to leave the Birac, Zepa, and Gorazde areas together with the Muslim population," General Mladic in 1992 intended that the Muslim population leave the Zepa area based on this document, didn't he, General?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: The population in general, regardless of their ethnicity, left the territories which were under the control of the other party. It is a normal consequence of a civil war. And this is what happened throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina throughout that period of time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, that's not the question, that is not the question I'm asking you. If you can't answer the question, say, "I don't want to answer the question; I don't understand the question." Based on this order, would you agree with me that it was General Mladic's intention that the Muslim population should leave Zepa?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: The express character of this order of General Mladic was intended for the enemy to leave the area, to force the enemy to leave the area. The order concerns the enemy, not the population, but General Mladic knows that the population would leave as well because that is what happened throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when General Mladic says, and I quote, "Force him to leave the Birac, Zepa, and Gorazde areas together with the Muslim population," he doesn't actually means what he said at all; he doesn't mean force him to leave. Is that what you're saying to the Court?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: No. I'm referring to what he explicitly requests, that is, to force the enemy to leave the area, not the civilian population. And the civilian population expresses -- the civilian population decides for themselves whether to leave the area or not, because that is what happened in Srebrenica as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, the order speaks for itself, so we can move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If I could have D167, please, Defence Exhibit 167, Defence Exhibit 168, and Prosecutor's Exhibit 364, volume 2, the intercept from the 25th of July of 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, General, this is the document that you've already referred to, and the particular part that I am interested in is where Colonel Cerovic states -- one question before this: Who was Colonel Cerovic?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel Cerovic was the assistant commander for politics, morale of the Drina Corps. He was the assistant commander to the Drina Corps Commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the paragraph that I'm interested in is halfway down, and in your version -- you have a typed version, I think, and I will read it, and hopefully you can catch up in the Serbian version where I am. It's about halfway down. And Cerovic says "all right," and then after that Uran or Obrad, Colonel Vicic, Chief of Operations in the Drina Corps, says, "And also literally that we are to behave in civilised fashion and that everybody is to behave like that so that nothing of the kind of problem we had before happens." Do you see that section?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, General, you would agree with me that the problem that he is talking about is the murder of -- or at least, the international press finding out about the murder of thousands of Muslim men after the fall of the Srebrenica enclave. That's the little problem that he's referring to, isn't he, General?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: No. No, that is not how I understand it. I'm not saying that that didn't happen, what you're saying, because it has been established in this case. It's just that this text and this message explicitly concerns the behaviour of the -- towards the column of civilians so that the problems which had taken place in Srebrenica would be avoided.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, General, if Colonel Vicic is aware of problems of uncivilised behaviour within the Drina Corps, and if Colonel Cerovic is aware of uncivilised behaviour in the Drina Corps, it would be fair to say that everybody else in the Drina Corps command was aware by the 25th of July of uncivilised behaviour within the Drina Corps; would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, I might agree with you that many of them knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do we have Prosecutor's Exhibit 364? This is, Your Honours, 364, volume 2, it's an intercept of the 25th of July. It's the same date as these two conversations that Colonel Cerovic has, and I will read most of it through, not all of it. And it is a conversation between General Milan Gvero and a certain Subara whose location couldn't be determined.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First of all, General Radinovic, who is General Milan Gvero in 1995?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: General Milan Gvero was the assistant commander of the Main Staff for morale, politics, and religious affairs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So he was Cerovic's direct superior? He was doing the same job as Colonel Cerovic but in the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He worked in the Main Staff in the same affairs as Colonel Cerovic, but there is no direct chain of command link because he is subordinated to his commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But they were both morale, legal, and religious affairs officers?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me read this conversation, and as I say, I'm not going to read all of it. S: May God be with you, General, sir. How are you? G: Oh, Subara, fine, how are you? S: I'm calling to tell you to watch out what you're doing over there with Zepa, not to let it be like Srebrenica, because there is talk that they slaughtered and rampaged there. G: They're lying, man, they're lying. S: Well I know. But watch out. That's why it would be good, there's this guy, Peter Arnett, he's there. G: Subara, everything's been agreed, an agreement was signed last night. We're going to allow everything. If they're smart, the ICRC will control it and an UNPROFOR representative will also be present. S: It's good you've done that in Zepa. G: But those of military age won't be able to go. They'll go to reception centres and they'll be registered. We're doing everything in compliance with international laws of war. S: Great. That's good. G: Okay. Thank you for the reminder, but that's how it's being done. S: Yes, that's smart, because they criticised us badly for Srebrenica. G: They're just making things up. What else can they do? There's nothing else they can do but lie. S: We also made a mistake by not bringing in journalists. G: We didn't make a mistake. We didn't. And I'm not going to read the rest. If Mr. Visnjic wishes to refer to it in your re-examination, he can. Now, General, the little problem that Colonel Cerovic is talking about and the orders which General Krstic gave are a direct result of this, aren't they? The VRS knew by the 25th of July that the world knew what had happened in Srebrenica; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: They knew, more or less, but the point is whether the people in Zepa could have known, in view of the situation. I never said that nobody knew, but I'm sure that many did not know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, the reason that orders were given to behave in a civilised manner in Zepa were because everybody knew in the VRS that the world knew that thousands of people had been murdered after the fall of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Srebrenica; isn't that a fact?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: You have Krstic's order of the 12th, when no one was killed, when he requested that nobody should have a hair missing from his head, without any pressure of public opinion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, if we can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Cayley, excuse me for interrupting you. You have already exceeded the time of the examination-in-chief, so perhaps you could try and organise your questions so as to try and complete your cross-examination soon.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I will, Mr. President. I will be finished within the next 10 or 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, let's go to that particular exhibit, Prosecutor's Exhibit 446, which is the particular intercept that you're talking about, and this is the exhibit between Krstic and Sobot. Now, first of all, General, you would agree with me that General Krstic is giving orders over the radio? Would you agree with that? Over the telephone, over the radio, he's giving orders?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: Orders are not given over the telephone; orders are given in a certain format and in a certain procedure. It is messages that are sent by telephone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is he giving some form of instruction over the telephone?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you'll see, halfway down, that General Krstic says, "Get in touch with these guys from the MUP, Ministry of Interior. That means you, your brigade, and them." So I'm right in saying that this intercept indicates that General Krstic is giving instructions not only to his own brigades but also to members of the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: No, he's not giving instructions to members of MUP, because if they were direct instructions by Krstic, he would have called MUP representatives to tell them. He gave instructions to his brigade commander, a brigade commander of the Drina Corps, to get in touch with MUP and to ensure regular conditions for the evacuation of civilians from Srebrenica. So he's not addressing himself directly to them, but via his brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So he's telling -- Krstic is telling his brigade to tell the MUP to do something; isn't he, General?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: To get in touch with them and to cooperate with respect to the organisation of transport, and that means traffic control on the road from Tisca to Kladanj.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, you'll also see in this intercept that Krstic asks for Kosoric, Lieutenant Colonel Kosoric. Now, you will recall that it is the Prosecutor's case that Lieutenant Colonel Kosoric led the first convoy out of Srebrenica to Vlasenica, to the point of exchange, and you would agree with me that this intercept in fact corroborates that view. Because this intercept indicates that on the 12th of July, Kosoric moved from Srebrenica to the Luka school area, to the tunnel where the Muslim population crossed into Muslim-controlled area; would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: No, I do not agree with you. I don't think that is the Kosoric you are referring to, but rather a Kosoric who is chief of the intelligence department in the command of the Drina Corps. This Kosoric is the commander of the Vlasenica Brigade. So it wasn't this Kosoric who led the convoy, but a Kosoric, an intelligence officer from the Drina Corps. That is how I understood it, studying the documents and preparing for this case and for my testimony here in this Honourable Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, General, finally what I wanted to ask you about is this: The Defence provided to the Prosecution a very brief summary of what you were to testify about today, and I will read that to you. Mr. Visnjic has that in front of him, and it says this about your evidence: "The witness shall, in the frame of the time that those conversations were allegedly held," and this is referring to the intercepts, "according to the statements of the OTP witnesses, put those conversations in context." That's what I want to emphasise: "Put those conversations in context with the events and with the position General Krstic held." Now, you stated to the Judges during your examination-in-chief today that you had been reluctant to give evidence in respect of the intercepts, and you gave a number of reasons why you were reluctant to give evidence. Now, when you testified last December, you also gave the Court a number of reasons in your re-examination as to why you felt you couldn't give evidence about the intercepts, and I want to read the third reason to you, and this is what you said at page 8448: "Third, it was impossible for me to follow the context in which the conversations took place, and first of all I have in mind of the operational context for me, to have a full knowledge of the situation and thus to be able to possibly evaluate what was contained in those intercepts." Now, General, you will agree with me that based upon what you said in December and based on the evidence that you have given today, you have undergone an almost miraculous conversion as far as the intercepts are concerned. Then you were unable to place any of them in context and today you are.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: You mean I have made a turnabout?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: Copernicus? With full responsibility for any inconsistency in my methodology, I have come, upon instructions of the Defence counsel, to comment on the intercepts, but under the proviso that I do not consider intercepts to be evidence. That position applies to all intercepts, including those I commented on today. How much probative value you will give to this, it's not up to me to judge. I will comment on any other intercepts that you may ask me to comment on, but under this reservation.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions for the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Cayley. Mr. Visnjic for any re-examination, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do have some additional questions, Mr. President. Re-examined by Mr. Visnjic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General Radinovic, am I wrong in saying that the conversations given to you to explain today, that is, these three conversations, were not shown to you before your testimony in this Court in December 2000?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: Which conversations? I didn't understand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm referring to Uran, Cerovic, and Bogicevic, these three conversations.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: You are right. They were not shown to me then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, was the reason for it the fact that the Prosecution disclosed some of those conversations only in January 2001 and that the Uran/Cerovic intercept was in notebooks and it was not used by the Prosecution in the Prosecution case?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could I now ask you to go back to Prosecution Exhibit 446, the Krstic/Sobot conversation. I think it is in front of you. General Radinovic, Kosoric, who is mentioned in this conversation, is his name Mile, the commander of the Vlasenica Brigade in the relevant period?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General Radinovic, this person called Savo, who is also mentioned here and who General Krstic is asking for -- actually, could you tell us who Savo is?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: He's the assistant for logistics of the commander of the Vlasenica Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is his name Sava Celikovic?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is General Krstic apparently contacting the Vlasenica Brigade here and, as the commander is absent, he's looking for the assistant for the rear?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In this intercept he's asking for Kosoric, but he's told he's not there, and then Savo replies, his assistant for logistics.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General Radinovic, the Prosecutor has raised a question that you did not testify about in the examination-in-chief, but I didn't want to object for the umpteenth time, and that is the question of the relationship between the MUP and the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown, please, Defence Exhibit D165.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General Radinovic, will you please look at page 2 of this document.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: Let me just see who is in the header.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have seen this document before, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you see it for the first time?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: During the preparations for this testimony.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us how many days ago?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: Shall we say three days ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell Their Honours -- could you explain the content of the second page of this document, without actually quoting from it, and could you place it in the context of the relationship between the MUP and the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: This document was transmitted on the 12th of July, 1995, and we see the time indicated here, 2210, I think it is, if I see it well. It says 2210 hours on page 2, and it was issued by Major General Zdravko Tolimir, the assistant of the Chief of Staff of the Main Staff for security and intelligence affairs. And certain units and institutions are being informed by General Tolimir about certain elements of the situation in Srebrenica. And on page 2 he says that they, meaning the intelligence and security sector of the Main Staff of the VRS, had informed organs of MUP, of Republika Srpska, which is stationed in Konjevic Polje, with the illegal corridor through which the Muslims of Srebrenica are breaking out - and this is reference to the armed people, not the civilian population - considering that they, that is, MUP organs, have the assignment to secure the Bratunac-Konjevic Polje route. I'm sorry that I didn't have this document much earlier when I was preparing my expert report because then I would have been far more convincing in my finding that the Bratunac-Konjevic Polje road was under the control of the forces and chain of command that was outside the chain of command of the Drina Corps. This is a very -- highly relevant fact, and I'm sorry that it was only shortly prior to this testimony that I was able to familiarise myself with this document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General Radinovic, who secured the Konjevic Polje-Bratunac road, according to your finding?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: According to my finding, the Konjevic Polje-Bratunac communication was secured by a special brigade of the MUP of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When we say "secured," does that mean on the dates --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President I'm going to object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I'm going to object to further questioning on this unless I'm given opportunity to do re-cross-examination on the witness. He's now speaking about matters which he did not address either in his examination-in-chief or cross-examination, that is, the control of the road between Bratunac and Konjevic Polje. I merely referred to an instruction given to the MUP in an intercept, and now my learned friend is essentially trying to get evidence in, in re-examination which he didn't want to ask the General about in his examination-in-chief. So if I'm given the opportunity to re-cross on this point, that is fine; otherwise, I would request that the Court directs Mr. Visnjic to concentrate purely on the issue that I raised in my cross-examination and not to expand it out by virtue of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Visnjic? Mr. Visnjic, let me remind you anyway that on page 45, line 23 of the LiveNote, you yourself admitted that this question of the relationship between the MUP and the Drina Corps was raised for the first time by Mr. Cayley, so in a sense, he should have had additional questions. But the Chamber feels that you should be able to continue with your questions, but if there are things going outside re-examination, it would be fair for Mr. Cayley to have the opportunity to cross-examine, in a certain sense. What is your opinion?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, as far as we have been able to understand, Mr. Cayley opened the door to this issue. I do not wish to expand. If we're talking about the Bratunac-Konjevic Polje road, I can withdraw my question about it - we don't want to keep the witness any longer - because this could open up a series of issues that the witness has already testified about. So let me focus on this relationship without actually mentioning the Konjevic Polje-Bratunac road, so I can withdraw my last question. But I do wish to point out that it was the Prosecutor who opened this issue and that we did not object, so in a sense, he's responsible for raising the issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is true, Mr. Visnjic. We agree, but we're applying the principle here of giving equal treatment to the parties and the equality of arms of the parties. It is true that Mr. Cayley opened the door so you have the right to enter that door, but it is also true that after that, Mr. Cayley has the right to put additional questions. So the Chamber is saying, you can continue with your questions, because it is in the interests of justice that you be able to ask all your questions, but giving the chance to Mr. Cayley to respond.
