So you may choose: Either you continue with your questions and Mr. Cayley will be able to comment, or you don't have any more questions and then Mr. Cayley will not have the right to come back to it, either.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'm afraid that we are a little short of time, so I think we'll stop there. I shall just ask General Radinovic a very general question raised by Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed, then. That is up to you. It's your choice.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Radinovic, is there a written document whereby the Drina Corps is issuing orders to the MUP? Have you seen any such document?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: No, I have not seen any such document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General Radinovic, my learned friend Mr. Cayley asked you about your conversations with General Zivanovic. How many conversations were there?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: One.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you discussed operational issues linked to Krivaja 95?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you cover all the issues? Did you have an exhaustive discussion on that particular issue?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: No, of course we didn't exhaust the issue. General Zivanovic spoke in principled terms, though I knew what the operation was, its scope, the forces participating, but I wanted to hear it from the man who was on the spot and who I assumed knew the most about it. And we ended our conversation regarding the concept, the effectives -- the main objectives, and axes, all the things that come under a description of an operation. I was particularly interested in the immediate cause, the operational cause for the operation because I couldn't put my finger on it. I couldn't find the directive, the document from which it would be possible to see that clearly, and I asked General Zivanovic for us to consider that particular problem at another meeting. And he promised that he would familiarise me with the main operational causes for that operation, that is, the Skakavac or grasshopper operation which was lead by the chief of staff of the Main Staff of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, General Hadzihuseinovic. Unfortunately, from that day to the present I was never able to get in touch with him again for us to complete that discussion. Why? I do not have an answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So after your first meeting, the agreement between you was that you would get together once again when General Zivanovic would show you or hand over to you certain documents, but since that first meeting you were not able to get in touch with him; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, quite correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. One further question in that connection. General Radinovic, at the time you were in touch with General Zivanovic, had the trial already started of this case?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid I cannot give you a precise answer, but I personally was just embarking upon preparations. I don't know whether the trial had actually begun in the sense of pre-trial hearings. I think you did have some contacts because I already had received documents from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. For how long did you testify in the courtroom regarding the operational circumstances connected to the Krivaja 95 operations?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure, but I think it must have been three or four days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have one further topic to address and it has to do with the exhibit used by the Prosecution, directive number 4, and I would like to appeal to Your Honours to allow the Defence the right, after having studied this document, to perhaps call back General Radinovic to examine him regarding some of the elements because we were really caught by surprise with this document. Otherwise, we have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But Mr. Visnjic, when do you think you could call back General Radinovic to address this topic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, that's a rather difficult question, but I think by the end of the day we'll be able to decide whether we need to call him back or not, and then perhaps we could notify Your Honours about that tomorrow. It's a rather broad and complicated topic over which I should like to consult the General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But the Prosecutor used only one paragraph of that document, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is true, Mr. President, but the question was a rather broad one, so I have to be cautious.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Cayley, do you have a response to this?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes, I do, Mr. President. I think, to be frank and fair, the question was a very simple one, a very precise one, and a very straightforward one. It was simply whether or not General Mladic had ordered that the civilian population be forced out of Zepa. Those are the words that I quoted, and I asked the General as an expert whether he thought that General Mladic actually meant that. You heard his response. So it's not a broad area at all, it's a very simple question about interpretation of a document. Secondly, the Defence cannot claim that they have been taken by surprise. They've had this document since the 13th of February of 2001. They themselves raised the issue of Zepa, and by utilising certain documents, sought to assert that that particular operation had been conducted in accordance with international humanitarian law. You've heard the examination-in-chief; you've heard the cross-examination. That document was simply put to the witness, to the Trial Chamber, to assert the position that as early as 1992, it had been decided that the population had to leave that area. Its relevance to anything -- any other part of that document and its relevance to this case, the Prosecution is not particularly concerned with. So I believe it's actually a very straightforward matter that the Defence can deal with now, and there's no need to call this witness back in a day, in a week, in a month. It can be dealt with now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Visnjic, would you like to respond?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then quickly, please; otherwise, we'll be in a vicious circle.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First, Mr. President, the use of these intercepts was resorted to when the Prosecution witnesses identified them with respect to date. Second, it was not the intention of the Defence to show how the Zepa operation took place but only to have General Krstic's personal position stated, expressed through the order. Third, if it is such a small -- a simple question, Zepa 92, and if the Prosecution indeed just wants to have the opinion as to what Mr. Mladic wanted, General Mladic wanted, Mr. Cayley said that it does refer to the general context and the intentions of the army of Republika Srpska as a whole to evacuate the Zepa population, which I consider to be a very broad context for the events. And it is in that sense that I should like to express all my reservations towards the intention of the Prosecution to introduce this document as evidence in this case. So it was not our intention to prove the general Zepa context. It is our intention -- and you can clearly see from that that it is a personal order and the personal position taken by General Krstic towards certain events, regardless of what those events were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, please. The Judges will confer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber is going to make a compromise in the interests of the parties, that is, that it will give Mr. Visnjic the opportunity of calling back the witness at the end of today's day, by close of business today, not tomorrow, but to state this today, in order to ask questions. If you do have questions, Mr. Visnjic, on this issue, you can ask the General at the end of today's day. That is the ruling of the Chamber. We must profit with the General's presence here. I think that this would be a good moment to take a break. No?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We still have the Judges' question, and Judge Wald rightfully reminded me of that. So shall we go ahead with the Judges' questions now before we adjourn for lunch. Judge Fouad Riad has the floor. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: General Radinovic, welcome back. I would like to have the benefit of your expertise to clarify a few things in my mind. I'll start with the last thing you were talking about, which is the order of General Mladic of 1992. I'm not interested in the order, which apparently is still under discussion; I'm interested in your answer. You said that it was -- when the order concerned, of course, the fact that the Muslim population should also be forced to leave Zepa with the fighters, you said, "The population had to decide for itself whether to leave or not, and that's what happened also in Srebrenica." Now, when you say the population had to decide for itself, don't you, as not only academician, as also a man of the ground, know that -- don't you agree that the population can be forced, indirectly, by some kind of terror, by the way of knowing what might happen to them if they stay, even if you don't tell them to leave? What do you think?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I allow for that possibility, that the decision can be motivated by fear, and in civil wars that is a normal occurrence. That is what happens. The population looks for protection from its own army and its own authorities. As soon as the army of another entity takes control, the population leaves. Of course, it is out of fear. They feel happier with their own people. And that was a natural consequence of the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina. This happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I'm not speaking of happiness. The fact that just a few houses would be burnt and a few shots gone in, don't you think - not even in former Yugoslavia; in history - if just terror has been expanded and the knowledge that that would happen to them, isn't that an indirect way of forcing them to leave, and that that's what happens usually, as you said, in civil wars?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: In civil wars, yes, that is what happened. That's what happened in Bosnia-Herzegovina as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: The second thing concerns the announcement of General Zivanovic that he liberated Srebrenica and he is now doing other things, he is now called to do other things. Also -- I won't discuss the fact that it's a bravado or not, because of course it's a question of context. It might be a bravado if he wanted to challenge the people who discarded him and there might have been a conflict which you could tell us about. But I'm also interested in your answer. You said, "There is no reason for us to say that somebody else was in command and not the de facto Corps Commander." Now, here it's a question of presumption. What is more evident: that the official commander is the man who is in power or that the de facto commander, whom -- I mean, you said your research indicated. Did your research indicate who was the de facto commander?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The de facto commander in this case, de jure and de facto, is the commander of the Drina Corps, and the commander of the Drina Corps was General Zivanovic. And all those who took part in commanding and supervising the Krivaja 95 operation from the forward command post are his commanding organs, organs for command, including General Krstic, who was his Chief of Staff. So they were all working within his command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You said he was the commander, the de facto and de jure, both?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But in your answer you said, "There is no reason to consider that somebody else than the de facto Corps Commander." You insisted that he was de facto. Did your research lead you that he was de facto?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Until what date?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: During the Krivaja 95 operation, throughout the duration of the Krivaja 95 operation. And I talked about him as the de facto commander of the Drina Corps that day, and he showed me a map and explained his decision, the combat positions, and both -- and the formations and the structure of forces. He spoke to me about all that with a map in front of him, as the commander who commanded the forces and who knew the situation. Otherwise I wouldn't have talked to him, had he not declared himself personally as being the commander. And from what he told me about the operation, I was quite convinced that he was in command of the forces, because he spoke about it in a highly competent and professional manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So he was your only source of information about that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: No. All the officers of the VRS and the Drina Corps that I talked to about Srebrenica, all, to a man, were convinced that General Zivanovic was the commander of the Drina Corps during the Srebrenica operation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And you had any documents or just verbal confirmations?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: I have a document. He signed the order for Srebrenica, the order for combat operations for Krivaja 95. The Corps Commander signed that. And there are a series of other communications that he entered into up until the 11th of July, including the entrance into Srebrenica with the commander of the Main Staff and part of his command, on the videotape that we have as a document, as an exhibit in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Judge Fouad Riad. Madam Judge Wald has the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Thank you. General Radinovic, as to the Prosecutor's Exhibit 446, which was the July 12th intercept, do you have that available? We've been talking about it. It's the "don't harm a hair on their heads" intercept. And again, reiterating that, it occurred, the intercept, on July 12th. Is it your reading of that intercept that the admonition, "Don't let anything happen to them" or "Don't let a hair on their head be hurt," applies to the people who were evacuated on the buses from Potocari to Kladanj? Is that your interpretation of that intercept?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and that can be seen from the whole context, not only from that sentence, but from the whole document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Right. I agree with you, but I wanted to get your interpretation of the 12th. The reason I asked that question is because later on, when we got to intercept -- to 167, and this is the one that you've been questioned about several times in which Uran says to Cerovic: "We are to behave in a civilised fashion so that nothing of the kind of problem we had before happens." And you were asked, I think by both Defence and Prosecution, what you thought that referred to about the uncivilised fashion or the kind of problem that you had had before. And I was a little puzzled by your answer as it came through on the translation on the screen, and that's why I want to make sure that I have it straight. Because you were asked what might be the reference point for the so-called uncivilised -- treating somebody in an uncivilised fashion, and you were asked what it referred to, and you said it was the column of civilians. That's the way it came through on my transcript. And that confused me in the sense of: Are you saying that the uncivilised fashion to which Uran is referring in the intercept is to the treatment of the people in the column, not the people in the buses? Can you straighten that out for me?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was thinking of the people in the transport column, not the people that were going on foot in a column after the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Well, I appreciate your clearing that up, because the word "column" has been used consistently in these proceedings, primarily to refer to the column of men that were following with parts of the Muslim army through there. So that would it be fair, then, to say that both 446 and 167, which we've just discussed, when they contain admonitions, one by General Krstic, but this one by Uran, that they were referring to behaving in a civilised fashion toward the people that were going to be bussed out of, first, Srebrenica; later on, Zepa? To the people that had, in effect, put themselves in the hands of the authorities and said, "We're going to be part of the evacuation"?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. Now, the second question is a little broader, but I'm very interested, as both a military person and a professor, in your answer. You gave us extensive discussion of why you were uncomfortable in having to give interpretations of intercepts. I'm just wondering what critical difference you see between the kind of intercepts that we have had in this case and other kinds of evidence which occur in all kinds of cases. For instance, people have to give, and especially in this Tribunal, although I'm not too used to it in my own country, hearsay. You know, a witness gets on and says, "I overheard a conversation between X and Y, and I heard X say -- but I couldn't hear the answer. I could only hear what X said," and that sort of hearsay. Or notes; people scribble down notes of conversations and later on the notes are put in evidence. Why do you think it's so intrinsically less reliable to be considering intercepts than those other kinds of incomplete and not perfectly attenuated, perfectly calibrated evidence that all of us get every day in other kinds of court proceedings? You don't -- if you have a brief answer, that's fine, but I was just interested in your observation.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: I'll answer that briefly. I belong to a profession which uses the method of inter-subjective examination of all evidence and facts upon Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. which it relies. That is to say, I acknowledge something as being evidence which is -- and fact, only that which can be borne out by everybody who I ask about that, to tell me whether the fact is authentic or whether it has been falsified, anything that I can cross-check. And until I am convinced myself as to the truth of a fact, I cannot attach great probative value to it. So that is why I am always doubting, I'm a doubting Thomas with respect to intercepts, until research, previous research has been done to discard any doubt, to leave no space for doubt as to the authenticity of what I have before me, until I have cross-checked it. And that is my attitude towards everything else, towards all other evidence as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. Now, I have a question about intercept 884. This is the one -- the first intercept that dealt with Bogicevic and Zivanovic. You told us an interesting basis for your interpretation of that intercept, namely, that the word "now" in your language, the word "now" has a much more particularised meaning than -- certainly than it has in our language, and that your interpretation of "now" in this context means just at this minute, but not before now -- or not before the particular time at which the speaker is speaking. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, immediately before the time the speaker is speaking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Right, right. I understood that part. Now, the part that I need to ask you about is, does that same word "now" mean this moment that I'm in right now as opposed to in the future, say, something a week from now? I mean, does it have that same instantaneous snapshot type of reference that you told us it had in that it didn't encompass anything in the past; until that moment? Does it have that same notion that it doesn't encompass something that will happen in the future but only something that is happening right at that moment?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: The word "now" in the Serbian language really means a very limited time. Now, if I am -- I'm saying this, when I am saying it, it is at the time that I'm saying it. If I say, "It's arrived now," it means it's arrived precisely at this particular precise moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Fine, you've answered that part of my question, so let me just give you the follow-up as it might apply to 884, and Zivanovic -- I don't have the intercept, can I --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not hearing you. I'm not getting the interpretation now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I say that your answer might apply to the intercept that I talked to, to 884. When General Zivanovic says in that intercept, "I have a new duty now," does that, in your view, mean that his new duty, whatever it is, is right now at the time; he has that duty right then and there at the time he is speaking? Not a duty which he may have to take up a week from now or two weeks from now, but he has that duty right at that moment?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: He is talking about the duty which he has just received and which he is to take over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Right away, now. He says, "I have a new duty now," so if "now" has that instantaneous meaning that you just told us, then he has that duty to take up right then and there?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: He has got a new duty, but new duties are assigned on the basis of a document, which means he has got a document for that duty which he is taking on. He says, "I have been given a new duty."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I think -- I don't have it in front of us, but at least as it was spoken or as my notes suggest, it was, "I have a new duty now." All right, I understand your interpretation, but I wanted to make sure how your reading of the word "now" would apply to both sides of that equation. My final question to you is, I just wanted to go back and clear up when I asked you the prior question when you said a column of civilians, you meant a column of transport of the civilians. Do you know from your research whether or not the VRS, any of the people that you talked to in the VRS, considered the actual column that was moving through the woods as military or civilian in part?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: Everybody I talked to considered that column to be a military column.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Judge Wald. General Radinovic, when you say that as regards the intercepted conversations you are a doubting Thomas, do you also consider yourself to be a doubting Thomas when it comes to your attitude as a researcher? When you start researching an issue, do you still consider yourself to be a doubting Thomas in the sense that it is your approach, methodological approach to the issue?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I abide by the principle of the so-called methodological doubt which means that I don't take anything at face value, but that I have to check things first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understand you correctly, General, you told us that the intercepted conversations can only be used as a hint, an indication, which may point to a corroboration of evidence. Do I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it has to be corroborated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you done that? In respect of an intercepted conversation, have you tried to corroborate that hint, as you say it, as an exercise?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I was not in a position to do that because I did not have the tapes, and without comparing each and every transcript with the tape recording, I don't think it would be possible to establish the correspondence between the two. And second, which is perhaps even more important, I'm not an expert for such type of analysis. I do not have adequate knowledge which would enable me to verify the authenticity of the transcripts, that is, the correspondence of the transcripts and the tape-recordings. It is a preliminary procedure that has to be applied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, General. Another question as regards the document of handover of duty between General Zivanovic and General Krstic, could they, too, be subject of this attitude of yours, the attitude of a doubting Thomas, as you said?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: No, they could not, because the handover document is signed by both individuals concerned, and the superior officer is the one who guarantees the fact that the document has been signed. It can be established very simply. You don't need to have any special expertise, any special expert opinion of that to be able to establish that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. When did you first meet with General Zivanovic? When was the first time in your life that you met General Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: I couldn't answer your question. I have been a university professor for quite some time, so he may have been one of the students, one of the listeners of these lectures. But I -- all I can tell you is that I did not meet him personally before I started preparing myself for this testimony. So the encounter that I told you about here as part of my testimony was actually the first encounter of myself and General Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So that was the first time you met General Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have one other question for you, General. How many hours did you spend with General Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: I think that the counsel for the Defence -- of the Prosecution asked me about that, and I said that I spent some time with him before the lunch and then after the lunch as well, couple of hours in the morning and couple of hours in the evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I know that somebody asked that question, but my question is more specific. Do you remember when you arrived and when you left? Do you remember the time of the day?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it could have been at about 10.00 in the morning and then until 4 p.m. after lunch, including the lunch break, which must have been half an hour or one hour; but I couldn't be more specific than that, but thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you have lunch together or separately?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we had lunch together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, General Radinovic. We still don't know whether you will be coming back or not this afternoon, but if you're not coming back, let me thank you once again for having testified here, but as I said, it's possible that you will come back once again this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me ask the usher to accompany you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will have our 50-minute break at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the Defence would like to tender Exhibits 167A and B, 168A and B, and 169. As regards the first Exhibit, 169, the Defence wishes to note for the Chamber that the document was produced by the Defence, but since the Prosecution has agreed with the method of collation of documents, with a view of comparing various statements and then considering them as one single document, we have availed ourselves of that possibility as well and come up with the Exhibit 169, which we would also like to tender into evidence. As regards 884, that is, the intercepted conversation between General Zivanovic and Bogicevic, we have reviewed the transcript. We did not object to the request of the Prosecution that the document be made part of the record previously as an exhibit, so I just wanted to inform the Chamber of that stand of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We have no objections to any of the Defence Exhibits 167, 168, and 169, and we would merely apply for admission into evidence of Prosecution's Exhibit 883, that being the document about which there was some discussion this morning, the directive for operations number 4. It was the document that I quoted from. I anticipate that my learned friend will have some comments to make about this particular matter, and I will respond to what he has to say about the admission of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Visnjic, let us hear you on 883.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the Defence objects to the admission of this document into evidence in this case for the following reasons. There's quite a few of them, actually. First of all, so far the Prosecutor has not disclosed to the Defence any proof as to the authenticity of this document, nor were we able to ascertain the authenticity of this document from simply reviewing it. As regards the second part, I'm not quite clear whether the Prosecutor wishes to admit the document -- to have the document admitted in its entirety or only a portion of it. Thirdly, the Defence believes that this document falls out of the framework of the Prosecution's rebuttal and the Defence's rejoinder in this case. Fourth, should this document be established as an authentic document, we would need a far greater amount of time than the time that we have been given in between breaks in order to be able to analyse it and to discuss it with the authors of the document since the person who seems to have compiled the document is an accessible individual, both to the Defence and to the Prosecution. As regards the context of the document, that will be also problematic. Mr. President, it is our opinion that the Prosecution is trying at the end of the case to introduce this by the back door, a subject which so far has not been discussed before this Chamber; that is, the issue as to whether the events from 1992 are connected with the events that took place in 1995. When I'm saying this, I'm referring mainly to the genocide charge. I must add that it is the position of the Defence that this should have been made part of the Prosecution case in-chief and should not be brought up in this phase. Furthermore, had the Prosecutor on his witness list had an individual who would have spoken about the events that took place from 1992 up until 1995 in order to establish that link, that would have been different. The Prosecutor has certainly had an opportunity to call that evidence and to present the document, but that possibility has been foregone by the Prosecution for the reasons unbeknownst to us. I see a minor mistake here in the transcript. I said that the Prosecutor "did" have an opportunity to call this witness and to use this evidence, so the witness was already on the list of the Prosecutor in their case in-chief. Also, I wish to point out that the indictment does not include the period of time prior to 1995. We also used certain evidence of that kind, but with the intention of linking them up with the 1995 context. Mr. President, the time between 1992 and 1995 was a long one, and I think it is quite inadmissible for the Prosecutor to try to use this document at this stage of the proceedings. And finally, the Prosecution case was long enough, and it is my assumption that all these documents, including the directive number 4, were accessible to the Prosecutor during their case in-chief. As to the fact that they failed to present it or to extend or amend the indictment, unfortunately, that cannot go to the disadvantage of the Defence and our client. What we want to say, Mr. President, Your Honours, is that the question which Mr. Cayley asked of General Radinovic may perhaps be linked in a way with the events that took place in Zepa. However, if we should start discussing previous events, then, at any rate, we would need a large amount of time in order to prepare ourselves for a subject which has now been opened by the Prosecutor. So I believe that in this way, the Prosecution is simply trying to ambush the Defence, in particular, in view of the fact that we have already objected to this type of evidence and this type of document in the past. And let me say once again, I think that the Prosecutor had ample opportunity during his case in-chief to bring up this issue, and it is not our fault that he has failed to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will give the floor to Mr. Cayley to reply. Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours. I will use the order that Mr. Visnjic gave, essentially, his points, I'll use them as subheadings and try to respond in the same order. The first point that my learned friend made was that there has been no foundation as to authenticity in respect of this particular document, and in the break I acquainted myself with the history of this particular document, and I can give you that now; it's brief. This particular document was part of the Krajina Corps collection which is a document that was seized by the Office of the Prosecutor. It was a set of documents that was seized by the Office of the Prosecutor in 1998. As you can imagine, we have hundreds of thousands of documents, and the decision on whether to translate any particular document from a collection is made by generally a very brief review of the entire set of documents, and then documents are chosen from that set. This particular document was not translated until December of the year 2000, and when its relevance to this case became apparent in January of 2000 [sic], it was disclosed to the Defence and I addressed that with you before the break. They received that document with two others in February of this year. So they have had that document now for over a month, and it's not a particularly lengthy document; it's about eight pages. So it can be said to be authentic as far as it is part of a larger collection that was seized by the Office of the Prosecutor from a VRS, a Bosnian-Serb army corps. As to the continuity of evidence in respect of it being handed from an investigator on to the Evidence Unit, that, of course, also exists, but I would feel that that probably is not an issue that is in question here. As to whether or not the document should be admitted in its entirety, which was the second point raised by my learned friend, I think it should be, because I think most documents of this type need to be read and seen in their entirety to see what the actual purpose of the document is. For example, this particular section is contained within an operative part of the document. It's a dispositive part of the document. And if only this particular section were admitted, that would not be clear from the document. It's a military order. So I would submit that it should be admitted in its entirety. Now, my learned friend has said in his third point that this particular matter is out of the framework of the Prosecution rebuttal and the Defence rejoinder, and I would say to the Court that the Defence themselves opened up the opportunity to put this document before a witness. The document -- the witness, General Radinovic, was making a number of assertions about compliance with international humanitarian law during the operation in Srebrenica and attributing that compliance to General Krstic. What the Prosecution sought to do through this document is to indicate that as long ago as 1992, the intention had been of the Main Staff, of the VRS, to remove the population from Zepa. Now, that intention may have changed. That particular operation may have been carried out in a more humane manner in 1995. I don't comment on that. But nevertheless, the Court should be aware of what the original intent was. That brings me on to the next point that my learned friend made about the context. It is important that the Court knows about what happened early on in 1992, and indeed, contrary to what my learned friend is saying, this has been addressed throughout. I recall during my cross-examination of General Radinovic, indeed in his own report he went back far, far, far behind 1991. I think he went back almost to the last century in some of his discussions. I certainly addressed events, early events of this war. I addressed the period of 1991 with him. I recall that myself in my cross-examination of early -- the early development of the war in Eastern Bosnia. So I think that point is erroneous and I think it is relevant to what the Court is addressing. Again, in saying it should have been part of the case in chief, I would repeat what I've already said. We are simply responding to what a Defence witness is stating in rejoinder about the manner in which a particular operation was conducted, the Zepa operation, and we are responding by placing a document which indicates the actual context in 1992 in which it was anticipated that operation would take place. I think I've addressed all of the points made, apart from the point that -- I think the 11th point that my learned friend made, which he said that we were essentially trying to ambush him, and I think that that is a misdescription of this particular event. The Defence have had this document for a month, as I've said, and I won't labour the point. They gave the Prosecution the opportunity to use this document in respect of one of their witnesses, and I believe it is a document which is of assistance to the Court and should be admitted into evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think that there has been anything new, Mr. Visnjic, from Mr. Cayley. Do you wish to add something to what he has just argued?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do, Mr. President. I'll be very brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please try to be very brief, because we are wasting our hearing time, witness time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. The Prosecutor has told us that it received the document in 1998. I can understand the claim that it is an important document. It is a directive. It was signed by General Mladic and issued by the Main Staff of the army. I cannot accept the explanation that this document had to wait a very long time to be translated. It is true that it is not a very long document, but it is a complex document, because it addresses the overall situation in the territory of Republika Srpska in terms of military strategy in 1992. Thirdly, just in passing, General Krstic was not a member of the Main Staff, so I don't know how this document can be applied to him. However, if that document is indeed as important as Mr. Cayley is claiming it to be, that it is on the basis of this document that the intentions regarding 1995 could be established, then that document should have been part of the case in chief. Once again, Mr. President, the subject of Zepa was not opened up by the Defence with these intercepts. It was the Prosecutor who used intercepted conversations in their case regarding Zepa, and Mr. Cayley used the intercept between Gvero and a certain Subara during his examination. It is not a new subject for them. They addressed the issue during their case in chief. That's all, Mr. President. Thank you. And just by way of illustration, if the Prosecutor needed three years, from 1998 until 2001, to reach the conclusion that this subject can be used in that case, then I just wonder how much time we would need in order to be able to address this issue properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Visnjic. I will consult with my colleagues. I don't know whether they have any questions. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber believes that the document has certain aspects which are identical to the documents that we are currently analysing in order to decide whether they will be admitted or not, so the Chamber will postpone the assessment of this document for some time later, together with the remaining documents. And the Chamber will make its ruling later on, because we have heard the arguments today and we will issue our decision together with all other pending documents. Thank you. Mr. Visnjic, however, there seems to be something that needs to be clarified here. Does this mean, Mr. Visnjic, that you are not going to recall Mr. Radinovic in order to reopen the issue, or do you still intend to call him back? Because both are possible. You can object to the admission of the document, but you can still, if you wish to do so, use the document to re-examine the witness on the basis of the questions that have been asked of him by the Prosecutor. This will not affect the decision of the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we have decided not to call the witness back for the reasons that I have just argued.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. Visnjic. So you're now going to call another witness. I think you have a witness waiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're quite right, Mr. President. I would like to ask a very brief private session at this point, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Let us move into private session for a few moments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are in public session. For the benefit of the public, the Chamber wishes to notify the public gallery that there has been an application for protective measures by the Defence to which the Prosecution has no objections. In view of the need to protect the interests of the justice [as interpreted], the Chamber has decided to grant the application of the Defence and the testimony of our next witness will be heard in totally closed session, that is, completely closed session. The blinds will be lowered down and the witness will be brought in. I should like the technical booth to make sure that appropriate measures are taken in order to have the protective measures applied.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. McCloskey will be taking this witness, so if I can excuse myself from the courtroom now after the departure of Dr. Radinovic and the fact that he's no longer going to be coming back, we hope.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that in order to facilitate the discussion, we have to take into account the fact that this proposal which I have given in closed session should be treated as a public proposal. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I do, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Petrusic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the record is therefore automatically corrected. Whatever proposal has been given in response to the Prosecution application, it was given in public session. The Prosecutor has requested the reopening of the case in order to have these reports submitted and admitted into evidence. The Defence initially objected to the admission of the reports in question; however, the Chamber believes that a solution could be found, a solution which would enable us to respect, globally speaking, the calendar and the schedule which has been in place for a very long time. We can proceed in the following manner: The expert reports submitted by the Prosecutor will be admitted into evidence as exhibits. The Defence will be allowed to submit as exhibits a report which will constitute a response to the said reports, by the 20th of April, at latest. It is clear, of course, that that report in response cannot -- can only address the issues brought up in the initial four reports and that it should be relatively brief, the report submitted in response. Both the Prosecution and the Defence are not allowed to submit to the Chamber any requests concerning the admission of exhibits except in exceptional circumstances, which is self-implied, and the parties will submit their final briefs to the Chamber by Friday, the 27th of April, 12.00. The closing arguments will be held between the 1st and the 4th of May, 2001. Let me also remind you in that respect that each party will have two days, maximum, for their closing arguments, and also that the Defence must be prepared to argue immediately after the closing argument of the Prosecution, and that the Prosecution cannot offer any arguments in response to the closing argument of the Defence. I should like to hear the position of the parties about this proposed schedule, and we should perhaps start with Mr. Harmon, because he has submitted this application, and I should like to hear his opinion of this proposal which we now make in response to his application.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, the reason I was hesitating is because in listening to the decision of the Trial Chamber, there was mention of four reports, four expert reports, and in our submission that we filed in our application for admission of this new evidence, dated the 15th of March, we submitted four reports, as well as a summary investigative report prepared by Mr. Manning. So in order to clarify the record, is the Court admitting the four expert reports that have been identified, those being the reports of Mr. Baryabar, Peccerelli, Wright, and Clark, and excluding the report that was also submitted, which is the summary of those that was prepared by Mr. Manning?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, it was simply a proposal, a suggestion by the Chamber, Mr. Harmon. We have to hear the response of the parties. If you agree with this proposal, it will be easy to change the conditional way of speaking which we used into an affirmative one. And you're quite right, the summary of Mr. Manning should be included as what we did with the reports because it functions as a guide through the overall text, and it has to be considered as part of the four reports. So with this remark, you can perhaps now tell us if you agree or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We agree with the proposal Your Honour has made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Harmon. Mr. Petrusic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have no objections, Mr. President, to your proposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So without wasting any more time, we can change the conditional tense which was used in our proposal into an affirmative tense. So this was, then, the decision of the Chamber in response to the request of the Prosecution. We have two more issues that I would like to address before we adjourn for the day. The first one has to do with something that Mr. Harmon mentioned concerning a number of documents. I don't know whether there have been any exchanges between the parties concerning this issue, but the Chamber has to make a ruling very soon, the day after -- the day after tomorrow, because we will soon finish the Defence rejoinder, and the issue has to be resolved. I should now like to hear the parties on this issue, and what can be done in respect of these documents; that is, can there be any exchanges between the parties which can help the Chamber in reaching its decision. And the second issue that I would like to bring up is the question of documents -- now, I'm in a quandary to a certain extent. I don't know whether I can deal with this within the framework of the rejoinder because the issue was actually brought up ex parte and is a confidential one, and we should move into private session for a few moments for that purpose. Let us move into private session briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So there are no other questions to be addressed today. I propose that we adjourn for the day, if the parties don't have anything else to bring up. We will come back tomorrow at 9.20 to continue with our work. Mr. Visnjic, any questions? No. So we will see each other tomorrow at 9.20 again.
